reason: The sources provide enough factual material for a surprising story with twelve supported claims.
story: In December 1988, Space Shuttle Atlantis launched on a top-secret Department of Defense mission to deploy a classified spy satellite. Just eighty-five seconds after liftoff, debris from the solid rocket booster struck the orbiter's thermal protection system. When the crew inspected the damage using the robotic arm, they were horrified to find hundreds of chipped tiles and at least one completely missing, exposing bare metal on the ship's belly. Because the mission was classified, the crew had to use a slow, encrypted video feed to transmit images to Mission Control. Ground engineers misread the grainy footage as mere lights and shadows, dismissing the danger. Commander Hoot Gibson privately concluded they were going to die on reentry. Miraculously, Atlantis survived the fiery descent. Upon landing, technicians discovered over seven hundred damaged tiles and a missing tile that had fortuitously sat over a thick aluminum antenna plate, preventing a catastrophic burn-through.
angle: Over 700 heat shield tiles were ripped off during launch, and the crew survived fiery reentry only because a single missing tile sat directly over a thick steel antenna plate.

claims.claim: STS-27 launched on December 2, 1988, from Kennedy Space Center.
The mission was a classified Department of Defense flight carrying the Lacrosse surveillance satellite.
Ablative insulating material from the right solid rocket booster nose cap struck the orbiter about 85 seconds into ascent.
The crew used the shuttle's Canadarm to inspect the starboard side damage.
Due to mission classification, the crew was forced to use a slow, encrypted transmission method to send images to ground control.
Mission Control engineers viewed the poor-quality images and concluded the damage was just lights and shadows, telling the crew it was no worse than past flights.
Commander Robert 'Hoot' Gibson and crew members believed they would not survive reentry and were going to die.
Upon landing, over 700 damaged tiles were counted.
At least one tile was completely missing from the fuselage.
The missing tile was located over a thick aluminum mounting plate for an L-band antenna.
STS-27 landed successfully at Edwards Air Force Base on December 6, 1988.
The mission was the third flight of Space Shuttle Atlantis.

disputed: Unconfirmed rumors of a secret spacewalk to repair a failed satellite antenna after deployment should be attributed with phrases like 'according to one account' or left out.
